title: Therapeutic frequencies in digital music culture: A content analysis on technical accuracy and the expectation effect (Yuvaci, Journal for the Interdisciplinary Art and Education 7(2), 2026)
screen_reason: Content analysis of 150 'healing frequency' items from seven digital platforms in which each item's title claim (e.g. '528 Hz') was verified against an objective external ground truth (FFT spectrum measurement). 138/150 (92%) did not contain the promised frequency, i.e. a share of items in a sample classified inaccurate/false, with a stated denominator. The author explicitly frames this as documenting the extent of disinformation.

estimates.country: not stated (content on global digital platforms; study conducted in Turkiye and includes the Turkish platform Fizy)
estimates.platform: YouTube, YouTube Music, Instagram, Spotify, Fizy, Apple Music, Deezer
estimates.date: not reported (article received 11 December 2025, published 30 June 2026)
estimates.measure_type: % of 'healing frequency' contents whose audio did not contain the Hz value promised in its title/description (FFT verification)
estimates.denominator: 150 digital contents carrying a specific Hz value (e.g. 432 Hz, 528 Hz, 639 Hz) in title or description and at least 10,000 interactions, purposively selected from seven platforms
estimates.definition: FFT (Fast Fourier Transform) analysis of the first stable 60 s at 44.1 kHz, repeated three times; content counted as technically verified only if the title-claimed Hz value was the dominant spectral peak within +/-3 Hz - all others counted as 'Containing Incorrect/Incomplete Frequency'
estimates.misinfo_def: "Scientific Verification and Analysis of Disinformation: To determine to what extent healing frequency content reaching millions of views on social media corresponds with established findings in music psychology, and to identify the scope of misinformation in this process"
estimates.source_quote: The fact that the promised Hertz value was found in only 12 contents (8%) points to a serious inconsistency regarding the technical accuracy of content marketed as healing frequencies. ... Table 2. Distribution of the technical accuracy of the contents: Containing the Promised Frequency 12 %8; Containing Incorrect/Incomplete Frequency 138 %92.
estimates.page_loc: Results and Discussion, Table 2, p. 98 (repeated in the Conclusion, p. 100)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Objective instrument verification: digital spectrum analyser and Voxengo SPAN FFT, three repeated measurements averaged, +/-3 Hz tolerance; the accompanying content analysis was double-coded by two independent researchers with Krippendorff alpha = 0.82 and disagreements resolved by consensus
estimates.moderator_quote: A total of 150 different digital contents were selected using the criterion sampling technique, one of the purposive sampling methods. The main criteria were that the content had received at least 10,000 interactions and included a specific Hz value in its title or description section, such as 432 Hz, 528 Hz, or 639 Hz.
estimates.notes: Denominator is a curated topical corpus (keyword set 'frequency, meditation music, solfeggio frequencies, healing sounds', engagement threshold >=10,000 interactions), so denom_selection=curated. Borderline flag is about construct fit, not about the number: the falsified claim is a technical property of the audio file (the advertised Hz is absent) rather than a classic health claim, although the author frames the whole genre as health disinformation. The complementary 8% (12/150 accurate) is the same estimate and is not given a separate row. The 150 items are not split by platform in the accuracy table, so no platform rows are possible. Year is the publication year; no data-collection window is reported.

missed_or_uncertain: Table 2 also reports 'Using a Pure Tone (Sine Wave) 9 (6%)' and 'Containing Only Low-Tempo Music 129 (86%)'. Neither is a falsity judgement (they describe musical structure), so neither is extracted; the 86% is the figure the author uses to argue the relaxation effect is tempo-driven, and it could be read as a QUALITY-style descriptor at best. The discursive analysis (metaphorical use of scientific terminology, chakra/reiki references, 'functional ambiguity' of 528 Hz) is reported qualitatively with no denominators. User comments were analysed by cultural reading only - the 'strong prevalence of reported healing and relaxation' in comments is never quantified.

rob.design: Criterion (purposive) sample of 150 contents with >=10,000 interactions and an explicit Hz value in title/description, drawn from seven platforms (YouTube 60, YouTube Music 20, Instagram 20, Fizy 15, Spotify 15, Apple Music 10, Deezer 10); technical verification by FFT on the first 60 s, three repeated measurements, +/-3 Hz tolerance; content coding by two independent researchers with Krippendorff alpha = 0.82 and consensus adjudication; no data-collection dates, no search-ranking detail, no engagement weighting of the prevalence estimate.
rob.item6_quote: If the frequency value stated in the title was observed as the dominant spectral peak within a tolerance range of +/-3 Hz in the analysis, the content was considered technically verified.
rob.item10_quote: Table 2. Distribution of the technical accuracy of the contents - Containing Incorrect/Incomplete Frequency: Number of Contents (n=150) 138, %92.
